title: Vidéotron Ltée v. Technologies Konek Inc.
frame:
Forum: Federal Court of Appeal.
Parties as styled: appellants = VIDÉOTRON LTÉE GROUPE TVA INC.; respondents = TECHNOLOGIES KONEK INC. COOPÉRATIVE DE CÂBLODISTRIBUTION HILL VALLEY LIBÉO INC. LOUIS MICHAUD JOÉ BUSSIÈRE JEAN-FRANÇOIS ROUSSEAU.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellants, Vidéotron Ltée (Vidéotron) and Groupe TVA inc. (Groupe TVA), are appealing from the judgment by way of summary trial rendered by Justice Grammond of the Federal Court (the Judge) on February 24, 2022 (2022 FC 256).
How the layers nest here: The panel is the author (layer 1). The appellant and respondent make submissions to the panel (layer 2). The lower court's or tribunal's reasons are layer 3, and what a party said there, as reported in those reasons, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellants, Vidéotron Ltée (Vidéotron) and Groupe TVA inc. (Groupe TVA), are appealing from the judgment by way of summary trial rendered by Justice Grammond of the Federal Court (the Judge) on February 24, 2022 (2022 FC 256). Among other things, the Judge held that the respondent companies, Technologies Konek inc. (Konek) and Coopérative de câblodistribution Hill Valley (Hill Valley), are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in the retransmission of Groupe TVA stations, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations. However, the Judge exonerated the respondent company Libéo inc. (Libéo) from any liability relating to the infringements at issue.

In this appeal, the appellants are asking this Court to find Libéo jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for infringements of Groupe TVA’s copyright under the Copyright Act, R.S.C. (1985), c. C-42 (CA) because of its direct involvement in these infringements.
Having carefully read the record and examined the oral and written arguments of the parties, I would allow the appeal.
The Judge aptly summarized the facts of this case (Judge’s decision at paras. 8–17). It is therefore appropriate to reproduce the most relevant of these facts for the purposes of this appeal.

The appellant TVA Group is a Canadian television broadcaster that owns and operates a number of television stations, including TVA and TVA Sports. The appellant Vidéotron is a broadcasting distribution undertaking (BDU) under the Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11. As a BDU, Vidéotron receives and retransmits a number of television stations to its subscribers, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

The respondent Libéo, founded in 1996 (under the name Technologies Sys-Tech) by Jean-François Rousseau, is a company that operates in the information technology and website‑hosting field. Jean-François Rousseau was Libéo’s chief executive officer until 2019, and Joé Bussière has been its president since 2016.

In 2016, while he was Libéo’s chief executive officer, Jean-François Rousseau began a partnership with Louis Michaud to design new technological solutions for hotels. To that end, they formed Konek Technologies Inc.

A few years later, under a contract with Libéo in 2018, Konek designed a product known as the [translation] “Konek box”. This box allows televisions in hotel rooms to perform several functions, including retransmitting a number of television stations in hotel rooms. In the years following the contract between Konek and Libéo, Jean-François Rousseau gradually disengaged from his responsibilities at Libéo and left his position as chief executive officer in 2019.
In February 2020, Jean-François Rousseau was involved in forming Hill Valley with the aim of providing a broader range of television stations to hotels subscribing to Konek’s services.

On December 30, 2020, Hill Valley applied to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to be recognized as a BDU exempt from the requirements of the Broadcasting Act while being subject to a more limited set of obligations. The CRTC approved Hill Valley’s application for exemption on February 3, 2021.

Having become aware of Konek’s television station retransmission activities in 2020, Vidéotron ran various checks in hotel rooms served by Konek. The results of the checks performed by Vidéotron showed that Konek and Hill Valley were using the Internet to retransmit content, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations, to their subscribers.

Therefore, on February 26, 2021, the appellants instituted proceedings in the Federal Court, alleging that Konek, Hill Valley and Libéo as well as their directing minds (Jean-François Rousseau, Joé Bussière and Louis Michaud) infringed TVA Group’s copyright by communicating to the public by telecommunication programs broadcast on the TVA and TVA Sports stations without authorization or without having previously obtained a licence for this purpose. On the same day, Vidéotron sent Libéo a notice of termination of the service contract between them for the decoders used to retransmit the feed from the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

Before addressing the merits of the case, the Judge set out the framework for a summary trial and then agreed with the parties that it was appropriate in the circumstances to proceed by way of summary trial pursuant to rule 216 of the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106 (Tremblay v. Orio Canada Inc., 2013 FC 109, [2014] 3 F.C.R. 404 at para. 24). Before the Judge, the parties agreed that the issue of directors’ liability should not be decided at the summary trial and that the debate should therefore be limited to the corporate entities, namely, Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley.

The appellants (plaintiffs) therefore argued that the respondents Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley (defendants) had infringed their copyright by retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations. For their part, the respondents (defendants) replied that the said retransmission was covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA and that the appellants’ (plaintiffs’) copyright had therefore not been infringed.

In his judgment by way of summary trial rendered on February 24, 2022, the Judge made the following findings that are not under appeal: (i)The retransmission of TVA Sports is not covered by section 31 of the CA (Judge’s decision at paras. 45, 100). (ii)Prior to February 3, 2021, neither Konek nor Hill Valley qualified as a “retransmitter” under section 31 of the CA. Therefore, they could not avail themselves of the exemption set out in the CA for the retransmission of TVA (Judge’s decision at paras. 53–54, 100). (iii)Konek and Hill Valley are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements committed by either corporation in the retransmission of the TVA and TVA Sports stations, where such retransmission is not covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA (Judge’s decision at paras. 95, 101).

The Judge thus determined that two of the three corporate entities concerned, namely, Konek and Hill Valley, were jointly and severally liable for infringing the appellant TVA Group’s copyright when the retransmissions were not covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA. However, he expressed the view that Libéo, the third corporate entity concerned, was not liable for the copyright infringements committed by Konek and Hill Valley in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations (Declaratory Judgment at paras. 4–5). In this appeal, the appellants are challenging the Judge’s finding exonerating Libéo from copyright infringements in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

It should be noted that, during the hearing, this Court exceptionally allowed Mr. Spicer to make brief representations on behalf of the respondents relating to subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) of the CA, even though Mr. Spicer did not appear on the record. Be that as it may, these subsections are not at issue in this appeal, and there is therefore no need to rule on their scope.

The applicable standard of review in this case is set out in Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235 (Housen). The standard of correctness applies to questions of law (Housen at para. 8), but findings of fact or questions of mixed fact and law are reviewable only where the trial judge has made a palpable and overriding error (Housen at paras. 10, 36).

This appeal raises the issue of whether the Judge erred in his application of the applicable legal principles. More specifically, did the Judge correctly identify the legal framework on which his analysis is based? This issue is reviewable on the standard of correctness, and, as this Court recently mentioned in Canada (Commissioner of Official Languages) v. Canada (Employment and Social Development), 2022 FCA 14, [2022] F.C.J. No. 72 (QL) at paragraph 109, “[i]f the trial judge conducts his analysis on the basis of the wrong legal principle, no deference is owed.”

Although the Judge remained silent on the issue of ownership of rights, it is not disputed in this case that Groupe TVA owns the copyright in Canada to a wide variety of programs. Some of these programs are produced directly or through its subsidiary and are then broadcast on a number of television stations, including TVA and TVA Sports.
paragraphs.heading_before: VI. Overview of the relevant provisions of the CA

paragraphs.text: Thus, under subsection 3(1) of the CA, Groupe TVA has, among other things, the sole right to communicate Groupe TVA Programs to the public by telecommunication: Copyright and Moral Rights in Works Droit d’auteur et droits moraux sur les œuvres Copyright Droit d’auteur Copyright in works Droit d’auteur sur l’œuvre 3 (1) For the purposes of this Act, copyright, in relation to a work, means the sole right to produce or reproduce the work or any substantial part thereof in any material form whatever, to perform the work or any substantial part thereof in public or, if the work is unpublished, to publish the work or any substantial part thereof, and includes the sole right 3 (1) Le droit d’auteur sur l’œuvre comporte le droit exclusif de produire ou reproduire la totalité ou une partie importante de l’œuvre, sous une forme matérielle quelconque, d’en exécuter ou d’en représenter la totalité ou une partie importante en public et, si l’œuvre n’est pas publiée, d’en publier la totalité ou une partie importante; ce droit comporte, en outre, le droit exclusif : … […] (f) in the case of any literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, to communicate the work to the public by telecommunication, f) de communiquer au public, par télécommunication, une œuvre littéraire, dramatique, musicale ou artistique; … […] and to authorize any such acts. Est inclus dans la présente définition le droit exclusif d’autoriser ces actes.

In CCH Canadian Ltd. v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2004 SCC 13, [2004] 1 S.C.R. 339 (CCH), the Supreme Court of Canada stated that subsection 3(1) of the CA includes the right to authorize any of the acts set out in that subsection. The Supreme Court also discussed the issues involved in determining whether copyright infringement was authorized. It ruled that to authorize means to “[g]ive approval to; sanction, permit; favour, encourage” and that it can be inferred from acts or indifference: Authorization is a question of fact that depends on the circumstances of each particular case and can be inferred from acts that are less than direct and positive, including a sufficient degree of indifference. However, a person does not authorize infringement by authorizing the mere use of equipment that could be used to infringe copyright. Courts should presume that a person who authorizes an activity does so only so far as it is in accordance with the law. [Citations omitted.] (CCH at para. 38)

In CCH, the Supreme Court was careful to point out in the same paragraph that the presumption of authorization may also be rebutted on the basis of the relationship that exists between the alleged authorizer and the persons who committed the copyright infringement: This presumption may be rebutted if it is shown that a certain relationship or degree of control existed between the alleged authorizer and the persons who committed the copyright infringement. [Citations omitted.] (CCH at para. 38)

In Sirius Canada Inc. v. CMRRA/SODRAC Inc., 2010 FCA 348, [2012] 3 F.C.R. 717, this Court expressed the view that CCH did not “necessarily [require] a particular legal relationship between the user of equipment and the person authorizing its use” to rebut the presumption (at para. 26). In other words, the presumption can be rebutted in other circumstances.

Paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA provides that certain activities are excluded from the application of the CA. The provision reads as follows: Communication to the public by telecommunication Communication au public par télécommunication 2.4 (1) For the purposes of communication to the public by telecommunication, 2.4 (1) Les règles qui suivent s’appliquent dans les cas de communication au public par télécommunication : … […] (b) a person whose only act in respect of the communication of a work or other subject-matter to the public consists of providing the means of telecommunication necessary for another person to so communicate the work or other subject-matter does not communicate that work or other subject-matter to the public; and b) n’effectue pas une communication au public la personne qui ne fait que fournir à un tiers les moyens de télécommunication nécessaires pour que celui-ci l’effectue; … […]

This paragraph was interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada in Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. Canadian Assn. of Internet Providers, 2004 SCC 45, [2004] 2 S.C.R. 427 (SOCAN), and recently by this Court in Bell Canada v. Lackman, 2018 FCA 42, [2018] F.C.R. 199 (Lackman). The principle that flows from paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA can be summarized as follows: an intermediary who is in fact merely acting as a “channel of communication”, has no knowledge of the content and allows others to communicate without influencing the content, will be considered a “conduit” and, as such, will benefit from the protection conferred by paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA and will not unjustly fall under the definition in paragraph 3(1)(f) mentioned above (SOCAN at paras. 90, 92, 101; Lackman at paras. 4, 27–33).

Finally, paragraph 31.1(1) of the CA contains another exemption that may be cited regarding certain activities of Internet retransmitters to avoid the application of the CA: Network services Services réseau Network services Services réseau 31.1 (1) A person who, in providing services related to the operation of the Internet or another digital network, provides any means for the telecommunication or the reproduction of a work or other subject-matter through the Internet or that other network does not, solely by reason of providing those means, infringe copyright in that work or other subject-matter. 31.1 (1) La personne qui, dans le cadre de la prestation de services liés à l’exploitation d’Internet ou d’un autre réseau numérique, fournit des moyens permettant la télécommunication ou la reproduction d’une œuvre ou de tout autre objet du droit d’auteur par l’intermédiaire d’Internet ou d’un autre réseau ne viole pas le droit d’auteur sur l’œuvre ou l’autre objet du seul fait qu’elle fournit ces moyens.

The appellants submit that the Judge erred in finding that Libéo was not liable for the infringement committed by Konek and Hill Valley on the grounds that the appellants did not establish the “fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order” (art. 317 of the Civil Code of Québec (CCQ)) required to lift the corporate veil between Konek, Hill Valley and Libéo. The appellants allege that they did not have to establish this, as requested by the Judge, because lifting the corporate veil and disregarding Libéo’s distinct legal personality was not one of the issues that the Judge had to decide.
paragraphs.heading_before: VII. Arguments of the parties on appeal

paragraphs.text: For its part, the respondent Libéo essentially argues that, given the evidence submitted to the Judge at the summary trial, he did not commit a palpable and overriding error that would warrant intervention by this Court. However, like the appellants, the respondents also criticize the Judge for ruling on issues that were not submitted to him by the parties. More specifically, they argue that the issues submitted to the Judge did not include determining when Hill Valley qualified as a BDU. According to the respondents, the Judge therefore did not have to rule on the periods that had not been specified and submitted by the parties at the summary trial (Respondents’ Memorandum of Fact and Law at paras. 29–32). However, since no cross-appeal was filed, the issue is not before us, and there is therefore no need for this Court to address it.

At the hearing before this Court, the appellants insisted that the issue of lifting Libéo’s corporate veil had not been submitted to the Judge. They allege that they did not have to establish this, as requested by the Judge, because lifting the corporate veil and disregarding Libéo’s distinct legal personality was not one of the issues that the Judge had to decide. For its part, Libéo concedes that the appellants did not refer to the corporate veil but asserts that the Judge applied the principle because the appellants argued that the companies were intrinsically linked or inseparable.

The parties’ memoranda at trial confirm that the corporate veil was not an issue raised by the parties. The Judge also seemed to have understood the position of the appellants (plaintiffs) at paragraph 93: The plaintiffs essentially contend that Konek and Hill Valley are one and the same. They also claim that Libéo is liable because it leased from Vidéotron decoders that, until March 1, 2021, were used to retransmit TVA and TVA Sports. Libéo therefore actively participated in infringing Groupe TVA’s copyright. [Emphasis added.]

However, the Judge then took a completely different tack to address Libéo’s liability. He examined the lifting of the corporate veil and the distinct personality of the corporations at issue. Ruling that Libéo was not liable for the copyright infringements committed by Konek and Hill Valley, the Judge was of the view that the facts did not allow him to “override the separate legal personalities of these corporations” and therefore to lift Libéo’s corporate veil: The fact that the same people are shareholders or directors of Konek and Libéo does not override the separate legal personalities of these corporations. The shareholders or directors of a corporation may create different corporations to operate different businesses. As I explained above, it is only in cases of fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order that the corporate veil is lifted. The plaintiffs proved no such thing. The close ties between the two corporations or the fact that on its website, Libéo stated that it founded Konek do not mean that the two corporations’ distinct legal personalities can be ignored. [Emphasis added.] (Judge’s decision at para. 97)

In fact, the appellants did not allege at trial that Libéo should be held liable for Konek and Hill Valley’s faults (fault of another) through the lifting of the corporate veil. Rather, the appellants alleged that Libéo was liable for copyright infringements for having directly communicated Groupe TVA’s programs by telecommunication (direct fault).

In adopting the legal framework of the lifting of the corporate veil on grounds of “fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order” (art. 317 of the CCQ), the Judge’s analysis necessarily focused on the issue of Libéo’s liability through the lens of the fault of another, namely, that of Konek and Hill Valley, while it was Libéo’s direct fault that was at issue. By introducing the lifting of the corporate veil with regard to Libéo’s liability, the Judge therefore applied an incorrect legal framework, which led him to err in his analysis of the evidence because, among other things, he was seeking evidence of “fraud or abuse of right” to lift the corporate veil, while Libéo’s direct fault was the sole issue. It is important to note that, if the Judge was concerned about the corporate veil issue, he had to ask the parties to make submissions on this matter and, if necessary, additional representations. Since he did not do so, he was required to decide all the issues on the basis of the record and the arguments submitted to him. This was his role (CXS Transportation, Inc. v. ABB Inc., 2022 FCA 96).

Thus, had the Judge based his analysis on the appropriate legal framework, I am of the view that, in light of the evidence presented, he would have had to find Libéo liable for infringing Groupe TVA’s copyright.

After reviewing the evidence, I note that the Judge seems to have disregarded Libéo’s liability by relying on the testimony of Jean-François Rousseau, who said that Konek, not Libéo, had always paid for the costs related to Vidéotron’s decoders. The Judge also accepted Joé Bussière’s testimony that he was unaware of the existence of Vidéotron’s decoders in question and that, therefore, the evidence did not show that Libéo was aware of how Vidéotron’s decoders were being used: The plaintiffs rely on a particular fact to hold Libéo liable. Until March 1, 2021, Konek or Hill Valley, as the case may be, picked up TVA and TVA Sports using Illico decoders leased from Vidéotron. These decoders were in Libéo’s server room and they were registered to Libéo by Vidéotron. I find this to be a very thin basis for holding Libéo liable. First, Mr. Rousseau testified that he himself ordered these decoders from Vidéotron and that the fees were always paid for by Konek. He also supervised the installation of these decoders in Libéo’s server room. Mr. Bussière, on the other hand, states that he had not been aware of the presence of these decoders or their use. Second, even if the lease agreement for these decoders is deemed to have been between Vidéotron and Libéo, there is no evidence that Libéo was aware of the specific use of these decoders by Konek and Hill Valley. Ultimately, the plaintiffs rely on the fact that the same individual, Mr. Rousseau, was in fact the head of both Konek and Libéo. However, this is not a sufficient basis to treat the two corporations as one. Libéo is therefore not liable for any copyright infringements committed by Konek or Hill Valley. (Judge’s decision at para. 99)
paragraphs.heading_before: VIII. The close ties between Libéo and Konek

paragraphs.text: With respect, all the evidence in the record, analyzed within the correct legal framework, contradicts the Judge’s finding.

It should be noted that Jean-François Rousseau and Joé Bussière have a long-standing business relationship and collaborate in various information technology companies. More specifically, they hold important overlapping roles within Libéo and Konek. Jean-François Rousseau founded Libéo in 1996 (under the name Technologies Sys-Tech). Libéo’s main goal is developing technological solutions and infrastructure and hosting servers and websites (Judge’s decision at para. 9). Its head office is located at 300‑5700 Des Galeries Boulevard in Québec. Jean-François Rousseau was its president until 2016 and its chief executive officer until March 2019. In fact, he then stayed with the company for several months, even though he had officially left to work for Konek (Appeal Book, tab 24 at 150–53). He was also its secretary‑treasurer, director and majority shareholder. He still remains Libéo’s majority shareholder with [translation] “ultimate control” (Appeal Book, tab 24 at 20–22). Joé Bussière replaced Jean-François Rousseau as president of Libéo in 2016 and remains its second largest shareholder. It appears that Libéo is a small business composed of two directors: Jean-François Rousseau and Joé Bussière.

Konek was co-founded by Joé Bussière and Jean-François Rousseau. Mr. Bussière is a director and equal shareholder with Jean-François Rousseau. Konek provides integrated TV, IP telephony, Internet and Wi-Fi services for hotels. “Konek boxes” installed in hotel rooms provide access to a large number of live television stations, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations (Judge’s decision at paras. 10, 98). Since its founding until September 2019, Konek shared the same premises as Libéo at the same address (300-5700 Des Galeries Boulevard in Québec). Since September 2019, Konek has been located next to Libéo at 302-5700 Des Galeries Boulevard in Québec.

After entering into a contract with Konek in 2018, Libéo played an important role in Konek. When it signed the contract, Libéo knew that Konek was going to provide its television services using its infrastructure, including encoding capture servers (Appeal Book, tab 26 at 59–61, 64–66).

More specifically, after signing the contract, Libéo was involved in developing several aspects of Konek’s infrastructure, in turn allowing Konek’s customers to have access to Konek services. The Judge also highlighted Libéo’s contributions, namely: (i) designing and supplying “Konek boxes” (Judge’s decision at para. 10); (ii) developing software for the boxes (Judge’s decision at para. 96); and (iii) providing the infrastructure and servers needed to operate Konek services, including “encoding capture servers” for television content (Judge’s decision at paras. 96, 99 and Appeal Book, tab 26 at 64–66).

In August 2019, Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron television services. Joé Bussière confirmed that, when the ILLICO decoders were being installed, a Vidéotron technician had access to Libéo’s secure room and that, as a result, a Libéo director knew that the server room contained ILLICO terminals (Appeal Book, tab 26 at107–08, 112). In addition, during cross‑examination, Jean-François Rousseau confirmed that he had personally given the Vidéotron technician access to the Libéo server room because he himself had access to it. He further confirmed that, as of the date of his cross-examination, September 27, 2021, he still had access to Libéo’s server room.

The evidence also showed that some of the ILLICO decoders hosted by Libéo were constantly tuned to TVA Group’s TVA Sports station and then retransmitted to hotels (Appeal Book, tab 24 at 148–50). The respondents claim that, even though the ILLICO decoders were rented by Libéo, it was Konek who paid for them directly, and Libéo [translation] “is therefore not the one who retransmitted the TVA and TVA Sports content” and, consequently, was not liable (Respondents’ Memorandum of Fact and Law at paras. 39–41). This argument is without merit. As a contracting entity for the rental of the ILLICO decoders, Libéo was responsible for the way it used these decoders, located on its premises.

The close relationship between Libéo and Konek is also apparent from a document from Libéo’s website that was filed in evidence (MC-5, Appeal Book, vol. 2, tab 14, at 564). The screenshot mentions a [translation] “case study” conducted by Libéo regarding [translation] “Konek.ai the connected hotel room” and [translation] “Konek.ai: a very powerful little black box”. The screenshot, entitled [translation] “100% made at Libéo”, also describes the relationship between Libéo and Konek as one of [translation] “partnership” and [translation] “alliance” and indicates that [translation] “Libéo’s innovation skills are at the heart of Konek.ai’s success”.

In this context and given all the evidence demonstrating the close ties between Libéo and Konek, it seems to me that, when the issue is analyzed from the standpoint of direct fault instead of that of the corporate veil, it is extremely difficult to find that “there is no evidence that Libéo was aware of the specific use” of the decoders (Judge’s decision at para. 99) and that therefore it did not actively participate in communicating TVA Group’s Programs by telecommunication. On the contrary, all things considered, it appears from all the evidence that Libéo has subscribed to Vidéotron’s television services through the rental of the ILLICO decoders. It therefore receives the signal, including the Groupe TVA stations, and retransmits it illegally through Konek’s services. Accordingly, I am of the view that the evidence has established Libéo’s direct participation, and Libéo is therefore not in a position to avail itself of the exemptions set out in the CA.

Finally, the appellants submit that, given the Judge’s finding that section 31 of the CA did not apply, the Judge should have ordered a permanent injunction against Konek and Hill Valley and that he erred in law by relying on too narrow a view of the judicial contract to justify his refusal. The appellants are not asking this Court to decide this issue as a separate ground of appeal, but to address it in obiter because [translation] “there is little case law on the scope of summary trials, and the distinction is not always clear between the concepts of a preliminary determination of a point of law, a motion for a summary judgment and a motion for a summary trial” (Appellants’ Memorandum of Fact and Law at para. 94).

However, I do not find it appropriate for this Court to address this issue in the abstract, as the appellants would like, especially since the parties confirmed at the hearing that the injunction issue was resubmitted to the Judge at trial. The Judge will therefore have the opportunity to deal with it more fully in his analysis on the merits. However, I would make the following observation with respect to this case: on the one hand, the Judge held that Konek and Hill Valley were jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements under the CA, but on the other hand he declined to rule on the injunction to end the infringement on the basis of the agreement between the parties regarding the scope of the motion for a summary trial (Judge’s decision at paras. 30–35). Faced with a summary judgment without practical effect, the appellants have paradoxically found themselves in the same situation they were in prior to the summary trial despite a finding of copyright infringements and will have to institute further proceedings and incur further costs to have this issue decided at a later date. On its face, this result appears to run counter to proportionality and the sound administration of justice.

For all of these reasons, I would allow the appeal, set aside the judgment in part, with costs, and render the judgment that the Federal Court judge should have rendered, namely, to declare Libéo liable for the copyright infringements through its direct participation in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations and jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements committed in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations. “Richard Boivin” J.A. “I agree.
